Do you know what's talking about that the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims only favour the Serbs or Chetniks, and then talks about the Serbian two regions, Republika Srpska and Srpska Krajina, signing some sort of a -- or meeting to --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to make one state, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was Mr. Prlic correct in saying that it made no sense for the Croats and the Muslims to be fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had correct, but he didn't change the thing that they were fighting each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on, there's a portion -- there's something that we inserted last night based on listening to the tape. It says: "I have to still insist on doubting your innocence. You control all those routes of middle Bosnia. Maybe they control also some, but you control the road. There is no sense for the Bosnian army not to control by you." So also: "They are rumoured that you control them -- you control, take them, 5 per cent of the weaponry that you smuggled in Bosnia, and cut telephone lines in January." Where did you get this information, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of the document. It's underlined and in bold?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it's another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm showing you a document, 1D 01555 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where did you get this information? 1655. It's the transcript, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay. I never had that kind of information. Are you sure that it's my voice or not from Erich Rathfelder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, listening to both of you, assuming that he did any speaking, the voices are rather clear -- I mean, are rather similar, so it's pretty difficult.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, does this --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I tell you something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even I was very much in Bosnia, but I was living in Vienna. Erich Rathfelder was all the time living in Croatian coast. So he was actually, from us two, the better informed from this kind of details, and this is not the language I use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Fair enough. Was his English about as good as your English or better?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Because there was no distinction.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has been married with American woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Doesn't say much. Anyway. Okay. Now, yesterday, you indicated, by the way, that -- that Mr. Prlic said that the Croatians had built this road, a particular road.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I looked for it, and it's not anywhere here on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something off the record, and I wouldn't blame him from building this road. It was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I'm just -- because if we go further down, in the next paragraph, I just want to point this out: There is some -- there is some conversation going on with respect to weapons or trucks and humanitarian aid. And in the very last paragraph, at the last part of the paragraph, they said -- Mr. Prlic is saying: "I'm not sure about the number, for instance, 15 trucks. They said that it's for Srebrenica. And five of them went out. Our evidence and Mr. Halilovic said it to us later that these arms were only driven to Visoko, and they were used during this war. What do you do in this ...? To give -- to give the arms to somebody who kill you? I think that we must have global sightseeing about the situation, but it isn't a problem." And then he goes on: "It is a problem only, according to my information, ... but for which arms Muslims fight during this war? All arms come through this territory, you know, it's very well. It isn't the reason." Now, obviously, Mr. Prlic is having difficulty expressing himself. Would you not say that? I mean, they're not complete sentences. I mean, we can get the gist, but, obviously, he's not as fluent as one would make him out to be. That was a question, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And what are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move to the next question. Did you verify this information? Did you look into it to see whether Mr. Halilovic had indeed said that five of those trucks went to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prlic is telling you that some of the arms that is coming through Croatia to the ABiH is used again the Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he's saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we looked at this indictment that the Prosecution drafted and it talks about, because on paragraph 40, it says: "In particular," they highlight, "in particular April 1993." So by this point, he's telling you also that some of the weapons that is coming through Croatia into -- to the ABiH is being turned against the Croats. Is he not telling you that, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's telling that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, based on that, you interpreted that he was in favour of imposing some sort of embargo; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand there was an embargo, but I don't quite see that when I read article. Your are attributing that Mr. Prlic, and then later on at some point you even mention. Tudjman at some point, that they were insisting on putting an embargo on the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say it another way round. At that time, there was an embargo. It was the whole former Yugoslavia. And at that time, there was the discussion to finish with this UN embargo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, the embargo --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that was the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The point, ma'am -- the point is this: You assert that Mr. Prlic is trying to keep weapons from going to Muslim fighters, and you are saying that he is in favour of an embargo. When, in fact, an embargo was already in place, and one would then -- could conclude - I don't want to speculate - but they could conclude, if they're coming through Croatia voluntarily and reaching the hands of the Muslim fighters that, in spite of the embargo, Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are allowing arms to go to the Muslim fighters because the common enemy was primarily, you know, the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the common enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is another question. So long this embargo was, the Croats, the Herceg-Bosna was controlling everything what was going to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were earning very much money with it. It's a -- war is also a business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- very well. Now, there's this -- this is the only reference that I have for Srebrenica here, which is on page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the reason I only mention this is because if you look at your -- your interview, Genocide in Central Bosnia -- this was P 02094. It just caught my attention. If you look on page 1, it's a Prosecution document. It's a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Usher, you could assist in providing our witness with P 02094. In fact, it might be useful to have all the documents, Prosecution documents, to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in the very first paragraph, you say: "The president of the HVO, army of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina Croats, Jadranko Prlic is a -- is as sweet as sugar. He denies any violations of human rights by Croats against Muslims in Central Bosnia and repeats the official propaganda according to which the Croats are the victims." And I mention this because that's why I asked you whether you attended the press conference because it would have been useful for you to have heard what he had said during the press conference. But then you go on to say: "The Muslims are using the wave of sympathy from Srebrenica as a screen for their attacks -- for their attack." Now, where in the interview does Mr. Prlic say anything about Muslims using a wave of sympathy of Srebrenica as a screen for their attack. Where does he say that or is this part of your analysis, part of your spin?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is it? Are these your words or are these words that Mr. Prlic said again probably off the record which is why --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Trust me, they're not in there. You can take your time during the break to look at the tape, but it's not there. Are you not taking some liberties with the facts or maybe putting your own spin, as we saw yesterday, with the power plant and the energy? Could that be the case?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could it be that you're confabulating then?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's confabulating?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Making it up.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or could it be that this is just your interpretation? You have no actual -- it's not on the tape. We don't have your notes. You never said anything about this being on your notes. So it's not on the transcript. So how did you get this, attributing this to Mr. Prlic, because after all you're trying to suggest that he's denying everything about the Croats. All right. We'll move on and I tell you -- during the break you can have that document and you can look it over. But let me move on. Okay. And if we look at 1D 01652, this is the -- the text of what Mr. Prlic said in Mostar on April 24th, 1993, the very same day that you had interviewed him. I'm not going to go through the entire text because we can all read it, but towards the end at least, if we see the -- I'll read the first paragraph from the top, Your Honours. "The peace plan for BiH has repeatedly been refused by the Serbian side, while the Muslim side obstructs that plan and when the Muslim forces that not so long ago were allies in defence against the Serbian aggressor attacks us and when we have to defend ourselves against them we are being criticised. Each move of the Croatian side falls under biased scrutiny. We get the impression that our evil, if perpetrated by our men, is multiple times greater than the same evil by the others. Why? Is it not because our wishes for freedom is not a part of the old schemes?" Now, when he talks about "our evil," is he not saying through this sentence because there are other parts of this interview, but he's talking about "our evil." Is he not recognising that the Croats are also responsible for acts, that it's not just blaming the one side, but he is making a recognition. Is he not saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's on page 4, the top paragraph. I just read it, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move on. And let me move on -- I think we have 10 more minutes before the break. If I can move on to the next -- next page, page 4 of that document that we were looking at, what is the transcript of your interview, 1D 01655, page 4. There's another insert you will see, Your Honours. It's at the very top of the page. It's at 00.30.17 into the tape where you say -- if we look above it actually. Let's look at the above answer. Our proposal it's much easier -- much earlier than VO plan. Our proposal is much earlier than VO plan. VO means Vance-Owen Plan. Hence my questioning to you when I started whether you were aware of any earlier proposals. Do you know what the earlier proposals of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were prior to the Vance-Owen Plan? Yes, no, maybe, I forgot?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether they were somewhat similar to the Vance-Owen peace initiatives?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, exactly. Now, it says here -- it says here that -- is the function of region with national majority will be with all human and natural -- national rights and at the same time as percentage of inhabitants. For instance, in Mostar 50 to 50, Travnik 50 to 50. There is a problem. There are no problems on mixed territories. I said to you before that more Muslims live in this region than before the war. Now -- and then you -- then your next question is: "You will not propose ethnic cleansing in mixed areas?" And he says, "No. Why? You know we are ready to investigate -- to investigate all of these examples. I said to you before, there are no HVO now in Travnik, Jablanica, Konjic, Gornji Vakuf." Now, do you know what exactly he was talking about when he was saying it is a function of the -- of region with national majority? Do you know what he was talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking anyway from common administration in mixed territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall exactly what the -- the Vance-Owen Peace Plan called for?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what the peace plan called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the problem was the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how was he interpreting it to you on that particular day if we look at this particular statement?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was of course interpreting it like it should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But something already happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand something happened. Something already was happening all over the country. But this particular individual, the one that you were meeting with, he was publicly talking to you, a journalist who was going to be publishing an article, and he was giving you his interpretation of what the VOPP, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, was calling for; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the moment when Security Council was coming and the whole world was looking at Central Bosnia and also Herceg-Bosna. Of course he was trying to make the problems a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's your interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's quite normal. But your making these assumptions; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you go on -- if you look at the entire interview in the context, you were the one conducting this interview; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not the one conducting this interview. I was -- I was there. I made some questions, but you are putting very much in my mouth things which came from Mr. Rathfelder's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. All right. You go on further down when you say, and this is the part that wasn't in the initial transcript: "Yes, I have my opinion. Establish Bosnia but there is to solution in ethnic cleansing." And the answer is: "Yes, I agree with you but I don't support establish Bosnia. I want to establish Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not Bosnian, I'm Herzegovinian. I'm not a Bosnian Croat, I'm a Croat." Now he's telling you this; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So he's asking for -- what he's looking for is a Bosnia in Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those two together?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say some kind of autonomy for Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, does he say anywhere ma'am, does he say anywhere -- where does he say it that he wants autonomy for Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He don't have to say it because Herceg-Bosna was already founded at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, where does he say it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Herceg-Bosna was founded -- I knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, where does it say that he wanted autonomy. We're talking about a peace plan?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Later on. Let's skip forward. Does he not later on say -- suggest that he wanted that Bosnia-Herzegovina should probably be under international supervision?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the international community was saying all along that Bosnia and Herzegovina should not break up the way Yugoslavia broke up; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here he is calling for international assistance to stop the war, to keep Bosnia and Herzegovina together and to supervise it and you're insisting that somehow you're interpreting that that he meant that he wanted autonomy. How do you get there? Do the math for me.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say so. About end of '33 it started --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. You had an interview with Mr. Prlic. You've judged Mr. Prlic. In fact, I dare say and I put to you that you judged him before you went there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you wrote a story based on what you wanted to write. And I'm asking you, based on what he was saying, how do you get to autonomy? You're asking questions or Erich but both of you were there, two peas in a pod, you're asking questions he's giving you answers. How do you get there? Based on what? Show it to me concretely based on this document, based on your tape. Show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the things which were happening on ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the fact that there was a Herceg-Bosna. And later based on the fact that it was not -- it didn't last to exist even in international treaties. It should have lasted -- should have last. It was already a long-living state in that meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was a long-living state in that meaning? Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you point to me one particular document on one particular day anywhere where Herceg-Bosna, any leader of Herceg-Bosna, wherever that may be, asked for international recognition, international recognition as Herceg-Bosna as a state and I'm not suggesting legally speaking that that is the ultimate in creating a state, but that is one of the steps that is normally looked upon. Is there anywhere, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never got that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They never got that far.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you know that it was -- you know that they were with their own plates driving around Europe. You know that there was some --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, was a central government functioning in Sarajevo? How much time did you spend in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a couple of times in Sarajevo, but it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- pretty difficult to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And how -- was Sarajevo not under siege?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And wasn't it a fact that Sarajevo for -- the government of Sarajevo for all intents of purposes the best it could do was manage a portion of Sarajevo and nothing more beyond it? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not the fact. There was also administration outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Like in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like -- like in Zenica, like in Tuzla, like in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall stop now because of the break and we shall resume in 20 minutes' time, around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Madam, if -- we're going to stick with this document a little bit longer. This is 1D 01655. That's the transcript of your -- of your interview, and we're going to sort of pick up where we left off so we can complete that point. At the -- we're looking at page 5 now, and Mr. Prlic at the top of the page says: You know, he talked against this plan; and after that, he signed it." And we're referring to Mr. Izetbegovic above that. We can see that a couple lines above. You go on to say: "He did not talk against the plan. He only said that it was meant," like you say, "for all the people in the area. It was not meant ethnical, but it was interpreted ethnical. And that what he says, nothing else. And this was what I meant before, that normal people wanted like this. Okay. This is now ours and the other side." And Mr. Prlic answers: "I say all the time, the provinces with Croat majority, provinces with Muslim majority. I did not say in any moment Croat provinces, Muslim's provinces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I never said that you were, madam. Now, that's how he's interpreting the Vance-Owen Peace Plan to you, is he not? And he's concurring with you, with respect to what Izetbegovic supposedly is saying; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He says -- does he not say, ma'am --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one small correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Correct me.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was discussing with Lagumdzija, not with Izetbegovic. And that discussion is -- is refer from my interview with Lagumdzija, not with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He says here: "Why he signed," top of the page, "Why he signed. "MV: No, Lagumdzija. "JP: Mr. Izetbegovic signed it. "MV: But, if we are talking Lagumdzija. Izetbegovic signed it... "JP: I know it very well. Muslim side have done everything against this plan after signing this plan. "MV... "JP: You know, he talked against this plan, and after that he signed it." Who signed it? Izetbegovic signed the plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic signed the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But because there is these points, it's not totally there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I'm asking, ma'am, is: Mr. Prlic is concretely here telling you that he doesn't see -- the way he sees these provinces, not as Croat provinces or Muslim provinces, as others may be attributing how the Vance-Owen Peace Plan should be interpreted, but, rather, he's saying that these are provinces where there are Croat majorities or Muslim majorities or Serb majorities. That's what he's saying, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And based on your knowledge, based on your interpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, that would be the correct interpretation, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't change what did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm just asking you about the interview. Okay? Now, we go on. He says: "This was official statement of HV." This is your question: "Yes, it is official statement." So now he's telling you what the official statement is, then you go on: "Tomorrow there will be decision. What will you demand?" Okay? Now, you're asking him what he's demanding, and he says: "Our proposal will be the same as in the beginning of the war. We did not change our position, and we try to be serious partner. If we sign documents, we should do everything according to the plan, nothing more, nothing less, concretely." Question: Do you know what their proposal was at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it at that moment, but I don't know if any more. It's 15 years -- or 14 years ago, but, of course, I knew it in that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he's saying that their position, that is, the Croat position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the same position essentially as that which he's articulating earlier on, which is his interpretation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. So is he lying? Is he confabulating? Is he making something up? Is he misinterpreting? What exactly did you take his answer to be, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first question: What is the beginning of war? What do you mean beginning of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the -- the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were there any negotiations at the international level that you're aware of --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- concerning the break-up of Yugoslavia and the establishment of various countries as a result of the break-up of Yugoslavia and the various republics contained therein. Were there any negotiations, international negotiations? "Yes," "no," "maybe," "I don't know"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question was because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I asked --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there was two wars in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am. Ma'am, please answer my question. You're the journalist, you're the historian, you're the analyst. I'm not. Now, I understand, in 1991, you were in Iraq covering the war over there. However, you're back in country now, in the region, and I'm asking you: As Yugoslavia is about to unravel itself, do you know concretely - "yes," "no,""maybe," "I don't know," "I can't remember" - whether there were any international negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. For instance, here in this town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know, as Bosnia-Herzegovina is trying to find a solution for itself - okay? - do you know whether there was a referendum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose for the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say, there was also referendum in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there was, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am just --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to know what Bosnian people wants, and this referendum was ordered in this town, in this peace negotiations September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what was the -- what were the proposals at or about that time that were being made by the -- by the Croats with respect to what should happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you recall --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum, I know even the result. The referendum was that the Croats and the Muslims were for independent Bosnia; Serbs not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, thereafter, were there any negotiations, ma'am, concerning how to keep Bosnia and Herzegovina together?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because international community didn't want it to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me please at that point in time what the Croat position was with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina? What were they asking for? What were their concerns? What were their aspirations?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted that Bosnia-Herzegovina exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what the Croats wanted.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the Croats wanted. That's what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concretely, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Muslims wanted, and Serbia wanted something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. At that moment. Did you ever review, analyse, or have analysed for you, the constitution of BiH, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the then existing constitution? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the constitution before the elections of 1990, but it was not independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a Yugoslavian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Very well. In -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina - let's try to keep it simple - how were the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims characterised at the time? As what?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Constituent nations.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Narod.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Narod. Very good. Now, would that be different than, say, a national minority?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is very big. A constitutional nationality, or narod, let's say, have exactly the same rights as the, let's say, bigger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's not -- and that's what I have been trying to tell you many times. It's not depending of how many persons. We have in Finland five, five persons Swedish speaking, but it's the other nations. So I know these things very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad that we've finally -- there's a meeting of the mind, so far, on this one. Okay? Now, if we go down the page, because this came up yesterday, and you seem to interpret it in a particular way. All right. Mr. Prlic, in the very last paragraph, he's saying that -- he says: "You know, I want to say something for Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yugoslavia is better than unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why? Because Croatia was in that Yugoslavia. Now there is border to Croats. You know, Yugoslavia was complex country. Now, in BiH, it is not a complex country. It would be unitary country. There are none country in the world who has more than two constituent nations," and then we don't have the rest of the sentence it. But going back to what I asked earlier: When he's saying unitary is better than a unitary Bosnia, were you aware, madam, that that term, the way it was used in context, in situ, what it meant was: One person, one vote. And as a result of that, there would not necessarily be protection to a -- a nationality. Were you aware that that's how the term "unitary" or "unitary government" was being interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unitarian government don't have to be interpreted like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- well, okay. Let's just say it doesn't have to be interpreted that way, but were you aware -- were you aware of that term and how it was being used? Okay. A rose by any other name is a rose. And what I'm saying is: Were you aware of how the connotation, what they meant when they said unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I dare say, and I put to you, that in order to understand what Mr. Prlic is saying, and in order to understand the aspirations of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have to understand what they meant by unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. So do you know how that term was being used at the time. You being a journalist, and then thereafter, after interviews, forming an opinions and writing about it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody interprets them how they want. But unitary country means -- means one country with one government, but it doesn't exclude that every nation is in that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But what I'm asking you is: At that point in time -- I must insist on an answer, ma'am. I don't mean to be disputatious, and it's okay if you don't know. It's all right. But I'm asking you: Did you know, in what fashion and what context, how they were interpreting the term "unitary"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were interpreting it with many different terms, because everybody is interpreting it in his way. I know that there were these which were interpreting it like this one voice, one man, or even woman. But not all people were interpreting it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's switch gears then. Can you - you covering the war, being a journalist, historian, analyst - can you provide us with one single proposal made by Izetbegovic where he concretely spelled out, where he - okay - the head of his party and the head of the Muslim nation - where he concretely spelled out how he envisaged the government and how he envisaged the protection of all three national -- nationalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you point that to me?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So is at least the Croats could say, "Well, now I see how I'm being protected." That what Izetbegovic doesn't mean is: One person, one vote. He has the majority, and therefore we have elections. They get the top positions. Show me one proposal?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any proposals, any official proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of any unofficial proposals?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was not in the negotiations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. That's my whole point. During negotiations, wasn't that the critical aspect between all three nations. They want to know how they're going to protect their vital national interest. Wasn't that the point?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's the point, but I don't see that the protect national interest is to kill the other nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, nobody said anything about that. We're talking about negotiations. I understand you're here trying to promote your story. Now, let's talk about the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person is no story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the negotiations. You indicated that you were never there, right, in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say Geneva. I said that I never been in negotiations. They were hold behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, they were being held in Geneva. I mean, it's no big secret.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but even I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's no big secret.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- even if I had been in Geneva, I wouldn't have been attending the negotiations, because I am representative of no Yugoslavia nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you could have gone to the hotel, for instance, where they were staying.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And drinking beer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, maybe rakija. You could have brought some home brew from Mr. Alagic, and you might even have asked for an interview. You didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I was not in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would it surprise you, ma'am, that every so often, one of two weeks, Mr. Karadzic; Mr. Boban; occasionally, Mr. Izetbegovic; sometimes others, would be there; and when they were there, they were in the same hotel where the negotiations were going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's a point to this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of that? "Yes," "no," "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware, but Geneva is not my area. It's somebody else who is covering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether it's your area, but here's my point -- and maybe before we get to the point, let me ask you: How did you get to Pale, because you claim, you are claiming, based on something that we don't have, that Mr. Prlic said that Boban is travelling to Pale, secretly to meet with Karadzic. And the point I'm making is: Every two weeks, he gets to see him in Geneva. He can talk to him in his room. He can talk to him in the lobby. He can talk to him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how do you get to Pale during the war at that period in time, because I dare say, and I submit to you, that it would have been virtually impossible for Mr. Boban to have gone to Pale, as you suggested that Mr. Prlic is telling you.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he would have to -- he would travel through Pale in the middle of the war, when he could just as easily see him and meet him in Geneva. That's what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting. I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm quoting, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're quoting. We don't have your notes. Your notes were written in Finnish; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your article that you sent off, was that in German or was that in Finnish?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Finnish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from Finnish, it was translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not translated in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do -- what I have over here -- that's exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are no articles, if you mean this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The interview.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you mean this what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. They are my material for Austrian press agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's not that what was published in Austrian press agency. But if you want to know what was published in Austrian press agency, I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what they ended up publishing. I'm interested in what you did. You -- you had a conversation with Mr. Prlic in English; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You claim that after this interview that was tape recorded, he said that Boban is travelling to Pale secretly to have negotiations. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, had already been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had already been to Pale. We don't have a tape recorder there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but we have two witnesses: Rathfelder and Kesavaara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I got you right now. Now, you wrote this in your notes; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell me exactly: What was the question that you posed, and word for word the answer that he gave you, because I know you said that you took shorthand. But do you recall the exact question?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- I don't recall the exact question but I can -- because I have pretty good memory, but I don't recall exact question which is behind 14 years. I suppose nobody can do it.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the topic was: The just solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was telling: "Of course, we have to contact Serbs to find a just solution."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it also -- it is in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. I agree with you. Well, isn't that a fair assessment? That, I mean, if you got three warring parties: You got the Croats, you got the Muslims, you got the Serbs - they're all constituent nations - don't you have to talk to all three parties?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wasn't that what the negotiators were actually encouraging the parties to do?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't that exactly what the parties were doing when they were going to Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not question from Geneva at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Hold on, ma'am. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan was in January; right? That was one of the last proposals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 2nd of January. We're talking now in April right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But this was an ongoing process, was it not? Was it not an ongoing process?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs hadn't signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were the negotiations, ma'am, an ongoing process? It calls for a "yes" or "no." And the answer is yes, and you know it. Just say yes.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I didn't understand the negotiation. I was thinking about the treaty. It was not yet in power. It was not valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were not negotiators trying to encourage the parties among themselves, all three together, in different variations, shapes, and forms, to try to resolve their differences? Were they not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not -- that's not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when Mr. Prlic is saying to you that we need to talk to the Serbs and find a solution, or we have talked to the Serbs, would it not be illogic -- would it be illogical to conclude that those talks had been occurring in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I suppose the topic was not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if they're staying in the same hotel, why wouldn't Mr. Boban have to drive through either Republika Srpska all the way around, if you know the map, or go through Sarajevo, which is under siege, and then go on the other side in order to get to Pale? Why would he have to do all of that when he could just knock on the door of Mr. Boban's room or Mr. Karadzic's room in Geneva and talk to him, and do exactly what he was being encouraged to do? Why would he need to have all these -- this cloak and dagger stuff that you claim Mr. Prlic has indicated?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was the question of this ultimatum and on that what happened 16th of May -- of April, because it was not the question of peace negotiation. It was a question of forced solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could it be --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ma'am, couldn't it be that simply, you asked a leading question: "Is Mr. Boban having secret negotiations with Karadzic in Pale," and Mr. Prlic responds by saying, "We need to talk to the Serbs"? Could that be the context of -- of the answer that Mr. Prlic gave; and then because of the question the way you had phrased it, leading it -- leading the way it was, you --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- interpreted it to mean --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I make no leading questions, but I suppose you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You make no leading questions. Okay. Let me just go back. If I could go back to one of the questions which I thought was -- at least it's somewhat leading to me. On page 4 where you say, for instance: "You will not propose ethnic cleansing in mixed areas?" Now, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not made from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- all leading questions are attributed to somebody else, not you?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know my style. I have lived with me very many decades already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I don't doubt that. Now, if we look at -- the reason I'd asked earlier about the notes that were ultimately typed up or sent that are part of Prosecution Exhibit P 02094 is we know, first of all, that you took notes in Finnish in sort of a shorthand, and then this is going to someone with a rather large name that appears to be sort of a Germanic origin?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is on page P 02094: Genocide in Central Bosnia. That's one. I can't pronounce it, but -- well, I could, but -- and I think this is the one that goes to the Austrian press?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with -- it was not in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it, since it's going to the Austrian press, these notes are in German.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are they in Finnish?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm making --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's P 02094. It's a Prosecution document. Do you see it, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we have some assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was a document that, apparently, you generated that was sent out on April 25th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- now, we do have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the original, if I could put it on the ELMO, and it has an ERN 0212-2152. We can just put it -- and there are many polyglots in the courtroom, and I'm sure they can help us out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it seems to me, at least, that it looks like it is German.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's some kind of German made from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is sort of your version of the German language?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my version of the German language, which I never have studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And is your German, may I ask, is it as good as your English or better?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have studied more English. But living so long time in German area, I maybe speak better in German, but write better in English, because I don't know the German articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. The reason I ask this is because on page 2, for instance, you have on the second paragraph: "Prlic does not deny that Boban would have met secretly with Radovan -- Radovan Karadzic," and you then go on to say: "According to his statement, it is necessary to talk to the Serbs in order to find a solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And the reason I ask that is because it's so -- it's an interesting way of putting it, that Boban "would have met secretly."

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Would have met" --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- as opposed to: He met him. I think it's the perfect tense versus the past tense.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I was writing this for Austrian press agency, and news agencies have a certain style. They never go so directly, because they are always securing their back when somebody is maybe objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. So you were hedging your bets?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not mine. That's the Serbian material. And if I give you - but you don't want them - the ones which were published in Austrian press agency, they are not even my initials. And this one, which we published even in my name, the name was false, because they were afraid because for my security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't have to secure my -- my back in that meaning. I was just writing it how I was used to do for Austrian press agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But those articles, ultimately, were edited by somebody?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were then edited by somebody, and it was totally under because -- and this form like this, no news agency article ever comes. It was material for them, and that's why I took the results with me this time. I have them. And the title is not "genocide." It is "from a destruction of a village," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you chose the word "genocide" when you --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I chose the word "genocide" because that's what the Venezuelan UN representatives told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You said that they were representatives. Could they be investigators and not representatives that were sent by --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Mazowiecki, the Polish gentleman who was in --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anyway, they told us that they were representatives of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, ma'am, I want to thank you for answering all my questions, albeit unsatisfactory at times, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I personally have a follow-up question to put to you, to follow up on a question put to you by Mr. Karnavas. I would like you to go back to the document of the interview, on page 4 in English. In the third paragraph, because this is a long paragraph - because this is Mr. Prlic's answer - it starts with: "I think that it depends..." In the main body of the text here, in what it says, he is demonstrating something, and he says this. And he is addressing himself to you and to your colleague the German journalist. And he says -- and this is his point of view, and this is why I'm drawing your attention to this, because I would like to see what you have to say about it. And he says, as follows, he says: "We had 17.5 per cent of Croats before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina," and he says: "Today, not more than 12 per cent." The two figures he quotes clearly indicate that 5 per cent Croats would have left, and he then puts a question to you, and he says: "In that case, this is ethnic cleansing against ourselves." And he argues that there are Croats in the government. There are Croats in the Presidency and in the embassies and consulates, and then he tells you that there are 36 representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina around the world, and there is no Croatian representative amongst them. Not a single Croat there or Muslims. And he concludes by saying: "It is a Muslim state," and he then says turning to the three of you, because a photographer was with you, he then says to you and asks you: "Do you agree with this Muslim state? Do you support it." He has made a lengthy discussion and then he puts a question to you, and we don't quite understand what your answer was because there is an empty space after that. And he then adds - and this is what Mr. Karnavas highlighted a while ago - he will add that he wishes to establish Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he adds, "I am not Bosnian; I am Herzegovinian. I am not a Bosnian Croat; I am a Croat." And then he asks you all these questions, and we don't have your answers. Did either you or your colleague answer his questions? This was the question I wanted to put to you.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose we answered, but I don't remember in which -- which exactly in which form. I think that we were -- anyway, I was pretty astonished of this statement of Mr. Prlic, because you can interpret it with very nationalistic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you don't remember what you might have said or what your colleague might have said?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have said that -- that: What you want then? What? Do you want some kind of federal state or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This interview you had with him took place in April. Seemingly, one could imagine that this took place before the 24th of April. Do you confirm this or not? Could this have taken place on the 22nd or the 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes, but I know that it was the same day when this Security Council came -- came to Central Bosnia. I didn't know that a Security Council is coming, but we didn't attend the press conference because they wanted to go as quick as possible to Central Bosnia, and -- and afterwards thinking it was the right decision. And all the stories, which are published from that, the first one is the first, 26th of April, in Finnish press, this interview. This means this would have been 22nd. I would have been sleeping very long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you had this interview with Mr. Prlic, Mr. Prlic knows that this interview he's giving you is going to be published, doesn't he? Does he know it or doesn't he knew it, or was this an interview --

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, he knows very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he knows. He knew it. Now, the reason I'm asking this question is because you told us that the photographer was with you, Mirja Kesavaara. That's what she was called. Did the photographer take a picture of Mr. Prlic? Because when you have an interview of a high-ranking personality and when the photographer is present, the photographer usually takes a picture. Why were no pictures taken?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several reasons. It's very possible that she took a picture from Mr. Prlic; but because it was wartime and 1993 had different techniques as today, it was no possibility to send the picture to -- to the press. And so an interview picture, when you are going to publish the interview, it cannot have a -- your pictures, but you have to ask only from international agencies if they have in -- in their archives. Today, the situation would be totally different because there's the digital technique, and you take pictures everywhere and you can make them with computer. But at that time you didn't have anything. You hardly had telephone. In all of Bosnia, there was one telephone, and it was in BritBat press office in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your photographer, I assume, was also your interpreter, because you didn't speak B/C/S. So the photographer acted as interpreter, even if Mr. Prlic spoke English. But when you met Muslim, Serbian, or Croatian high-ranking officials, I assume you needed an interpreter, and I assume your photographer acted as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my photographer is an Finn, Finnish woman, and she knows her Balkan languages still less than I. She was just helping me in many practical things and taking the photos, but not interpreting. The interpreter we got from press offices or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you had an interpreter, this interpreter was provided by the press agency, and it was provided by the HVO, if you were on the HVO side, or provided by the ABiH press office, if you were on the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, yes. But when we were, for instance, interviewing Hadzihasanovic, with us was a Croatian woman, Bosiljka Sedli [phoen], who was the chief of south-west European cultural organisation in Berlin. She was travelling with us, so she was totally outside of any political influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two more questions. Now, this is my last but one. The cassette stops at a certain point. After the tape stops, there's a discussion with Mr. Prlic, including, as you told us, talk about the so-called secret interview between Mr. Boban in Pale -- with Mr. Boban in Pale. Does that part of the interview count as, what they call in journalist terms, "off the record"?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was never told that we shouldn't -- should not publish anything, because if somebody is telling that I tell this you, that it's off the record, don't publish it, so it won't be published. It was just -- we had finished, and then after finishing you still exchange some words, and this time they were important words. I know it from my notes because -- because they were there, and that's why they are also in that protocol I give 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning Defence counsel showed you -- let me quote the number. 1D 01652. This exhibit is a letter that Mr. Prlic was about to send to the president of the peace conference on former Yugoslavia. If you still have this document on the table, I'd like you to take a look at it now. In this document it appears that the main reason for writing this letter is the way the media are treating Herceg-Bosna. Right from the first paragraph of this letter this comes up. This document expresses on the part of Mr. Prlic that he's unhappy about the media. According to him, and as this document states, the media are not fairly telling what's going on. The media are biased. They persistently present the HVO from a certain angle and the Muslims from another more positive angle. This is what Mr. Prlic appears to be saying in that letter. Now, this is an important letter. It's nearly three pages long, and it covers several issues. I'm not going to treat all these issues now. But on the very next day after meeting you, Mr. Prlic tells at a high level -- he tells people that the media are not being objective about what's going on. Now, when you met him, did he also tell you this, complain about this to you? Did he ask you to be more neutral, to be more objective? Did he ask you to give fair treatment to his point of view and not merely voice a biased or otherwise untruthful point of view? When you were interviewing him, were you trying to take into account the fact that Mr. Prlic might have worries about your objectivity?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in this point I have to give Mr. Prlic some right, because English media was very much against Herceg-Bosna from the beginning on, and -- but it was not only Herceg-Bosna problem. It was also a big problem already in -- in Croatian war. Some media was just thinking the times of Ante Pavelic, and -- and that's why he had his concern. But we were representing Finnish, German, and Austrian medias, which were actually not blamed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To conclude then, yesterday we also looked at your article as you sent it to the Austrian press agency. This article is based on the interview that you had with Mr. Prlic, and on the third page of this document, which is P 2094, you raise the subject of Ahmici entitled in this document, "The Ahmici Genocide," and you told us, you told Mr. Karnavas that that was the responsibility of the press agency, that they meddle with the titles. You gave us many details about that. But in this document you explain more or less what had happened in Ahmici and, as I recall, you told us that you had seen the village with your own eyes. You saw the smoking ruins. That's what you told us earlier today. But, Witness, when you wrote this paper, did you ever wonder whether there were other villages that had been treated similarly, particularly Muslim villages, or Croat villages? Did it occur to you that perhaps there were also Croat villages that had been subjected to this type of treatment? Upon reading these paragraphs, there's no reference to the possibility of Croat villages having suffered in the same way?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of other villages, very aware. If you read this material which I gave Austrian press agency, the fourth capital it is telling about the refugees in the house where we were living. There were refugees from many, many villages, and also from the other side of the road, from Vitez and Old Vitez was under siege. Yes, I knew of dozens of Muslim villages which were burning. From Croat villages which may have been burning, I didn't know anything. I just met these two Croat women which were claiming that their village would have been burnt, but -- but I don't know if it was -- if it was true. Anyway, it was Muslim villages which were burning at that time. I don't know how many of them, but very many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But one of the accused as it happens, General Praljak, has shown us evidence. He drew a general picture, a map on which he showed us certain villages, Croat villages, that were subjected to the same treatment as Ahmici. Violence, destruction, plunder, that sort of thing. And out of this document there is a village called Trusina, T-r-u-s-i-n-a, which just a few days prior to these events were -- was attacked similarly. Had you heard about this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have seen burnt Croat villages, but it was later. It was first in the winter of 1994 when I just took the old road to Tuzla. They were trying to prevent me, but they were young soldiers and I was not listening. And then I realised why. There were from Muslims destroyed Croat villages. I don't know when they were destroyed, but there were at least three of them. Somebody told that it was an advance from the place called Stupni Do, which was near Vitez where Croats had made something like in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you have heard, say before April 25th, that some Muslim -- excuse me, some Croat villages had been -- had suffered in the same way as Ahmici, would you in fact have told this in your article dated April 25th?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would have told when I would have had little bit better information about it, but two women which were to me not very reliable for the British press office was not enough, and I couldn't drive in surroundings to find these villages because it was extremely unhealthy. You could have blood poisoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's nearly 12.00. We are going to take a 20-minute break, following which the hearing will resume, and I think that Mr. Petkovic's Defence counsel and then the Praljak Defence counsel will be asking you questions, and there may be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: See you again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume. Mr. Praljak's Defence. Mr. Kovacic or Mr. Praljak, who is asking the questions? Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Praljak will be asking the questions in the cross-examination. There are several portions which directly or indirectly refer to certain events which he has direct connection to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation? Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, I don't know whether you want me to repeat everything that I said, but I think that there are grounds - yes, thank you - there are grounds in conformity with your ruling and decision in view of the topics raised by the witness, certain topics especially, which directly or indirectly have an effect on the events that General Praljak knew about or was involved in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As the Bench is just telling me, Mr. Kovacic, you know that the Chamber has made a decision on such situations. We have given a decision which has been confirm. We authorise the accused to ask his own questions on technical subjects on which he has knowledge or when he is personally concerned by the witness's statement. Now, from what you're saying, I understand that he is going to ask questions on technical subjects that he has particular knowledge of. Is that right, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. You're quite right, Your Honour, Mr. President. I'd just like to add that bearing in mind, of course, the decision of the Appeals Chamber and the ruling of this Trial Chamber, I would say that they are identical because they confirm at the second instance what you have already ruled at first instance. So the practice today -- and we have seen that the question comes with the interpretation of your ruling, but we are satisfied with that practice because it is in conformity with the rights of the accused in these proceedings. So it was in keeping with your decision that I put forward the reasons and that it was based on those grounds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to interrupt at this stage. The Prosecution would, at this stage, just wish to lodge its objection, in general, to Mr. Praljak proceeding with cross-examination. With reference, Your Honour, to the Appeals Chamber's decision on Praljak's appeal on the Trial Chamber's 10 May 2007 decision on the mode of interrogating witnesses, which was rendered on the 24th of August, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber -- or the Appeals Chamber referred, with affirmation, basically, to various aspects of the Trial Chamber's decision of 10 May 2007. And if I may very briefly refer to three aspects: In paragraph 9 of the Appeals Chamber decision, it says: "In the light of the above reasoning, the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that there was good reason for the Trial Chamber to determine that a stricter application of Guideline C was justified in order to protect the rights of the appellant's co-accused to a fair and expeditious trial as well as the rights of the appellant," which is Mr. Praljak. And then if we look at paragraph 11 of the Appeals Chamber, second sentence: "Rather, the impugned decision held that in the interests of a fair and expeditious trial for the appellant and his co-accused, the right of the appellant to participate directly would be subject to the restrictions identified to avoid the appellant wasting Court time. And, finally, paragraph 13, second sentence: "The Trial Chamber made quite clear that the appellant's lack of legal experience meant that his interventions were of little or no value to his defence." And on the following page: "On the basis of the foregoing, the Appeals Chamber dismiss the appeal." Your Honour, in light of this, the Prosecution position is that the guideline provides, specifically Guideline C, that only under exceptional circumstances will the accused be able to cross-examine. And in this instance, we're talking about a journalist, not a military expert. She's not testifying about military matters. And under those circumstances, the Prosecution has difficulty to see what the exceptional circumstances would be justifying Mr. Praljak cross-examining. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has given a decision on May 10, 2007, and that decision was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. In paragraph 12, the Chamber said that exceptional circumstances may be particularly connected with the examination of events to which an accused has participated personally or the examination of questions, subjects on which the accused has specific competencies. An accused who wishes to take the floor will explain to the Bench the reasons why such circumstances -- exceptional circumstances prevail. Now, we have just been told that there were exceptional circumstances; and if Mr. Praljak chooses to ask questions, he is going to ask the witness to touch upon subjects on which he was -- in which he was personally involved or technical issues. Now, Mr. Praljak, there may be very deep disagreements here at the Bench.
