My position, which I have expressed on several occasions, is that a witness may be cross-examined by an accused, but the other members of the Bench do not necessarily agree with me. Now, Mr. Praljak, what then are the exceptional circumstances? What then are the specific competencies or the specific events that justify that you should put your own questions in the cross-examination? Let the Bench deliberate on that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness. Here are the subjects: The lady, quite obviously, is a war correspondent and was present in the war, and she spoke about the situation in Mostar in June 1992, and which mosques were destroyed and by whom and which were damaged, and so on. She spoke about the Turbe or the defence of Travnik, the route of salvation. And as I was there at the time, I think I can address the issue. She also spoke about Drnis, Ivan Drnis, who was an HVO representative, and I can ask her whether she had ever seen him. The lady also spoke about the electric power plants in Jablanica and their importance; and as an electric technical engineer, I know the area, so I can question her on that. The lady also went on to speak about the siege of Mostar, so I can ask her how she knows that it was a siege, where the lines were, whether she went there. Then she said that she had seen the Croats of Vitez shelling Zenica and that anti-aircraft artillery was targeting a Muslim village. It was in the statement. Anti-aircraft artillery was mentioned, belonging to the HVO, targeting a village where there were only civilians. She mentioned that, too. Then she mentioned the H-O-S, HOS, and what its role was, and which units belonged to HOS, and who was in command of the HOS units, and so on and so forth. All these are facts mentioned by the witness here in court, and I know enough about the facts to cross-examine her, to ask her what she knows about all these things, exactly what her knowledge of these matters is. And I think that is sufficient grounds for me to be able to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Based on the list of questions that you have just presented to us, the Bench considers that a number of these subjects could have been dealt with. The questions could have been asked by your counsel, but the Bench also notes that there are a few technical issues that may be relevant to your specific competencies. That includes the question of electricity and that of the HOS since you were present in Mostar. I want you to ask your technical questions only. The remaining questions may be asked by Mr. Kovacic. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I consider that I know the areas very well. I took part in events in them, but I will abide by the Trial Chamber's ruling, of course. I'd just like to mention, in this regard, that I deserve justice. I don't have to plead for justice. And in order to arrive at justice and the truth, you yourself, Judge Antonetti, said we must find the truth with a capital "T". Now, I, once again, claim that certain details mentioned by the lady, nobody knows about them better than I do. So nobody is better placed to ask the lady about what facts she had at her disposal, what insight and access she had to various material from a second source, and so on. So I'd like to go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, in June -- and in the interests of time, madam, I'll ask you simple questions and please give me simple questions wherever possible. You were in Mostar in June 1992, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many Muslims there were in the HVO in percentages?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there was pretty many.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, please, how many mosques were there in Mostar before the Serbs shelled the city? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is not within the scope that was mandated by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I say something? I think that it is a technical question when somebody speaks about the number of certain types of facilities, in this case mosques, especially because the accused spent a large portion of his life in Mostar as a young man, before the war and also during the war. So as to the number of mosques, this is something that he knows about, facts on the ground. And that is a technical question, and he is best placed to know these matters. The Accused Praljak is best placed to know that. Who can know this better than him, if she says, "I know this mosque. I don't know that mosque." So it's only the Accused Praljak, with all due respect to other people from Mostar, he can say, "No, that mosque wasn't there. It was here." So these are technical questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may go ahead, Mr. Praljak, on the mosques, because the witness did raise the subject of a mosque. So, Mr. Praljak, go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, do you know how many mosques there were in Mostar before the Serbs attacked it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- I don't know exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me which mosques you visited when you were there in June 1992, and how -- what was the damage done to those mosques? So how many mosques did you visit?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't visit any mosque. I am a woman and Christian. It's not very possible. Damages were obviously from shelling or also from small-weapons fire. I could see these damages outside, or broken minarets, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, do you know that of the 14 mosques which existed, 12 were partially or completely destroyed by Serb shelling?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it was destroyed by Serb shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Now, you said that, in the autumn of 1992, you went from Tomislavgrad to Prozor and Rama, taking the road, the Route of Salvation. Do you know that the HVO made this road, Route of Salvation, so that the refugees which -- who had been expelled from the Serbs would be allowed to go that way and that they wanted to establish communication?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has to object. Mr. Praljak is ignoring the order of the Chamber that he's allowed to speak on the HOS, electricity, and on mosques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic. If the Prosecution objects every time, we're going to waste a lot of time. This demonstrates the absurdity of this system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you've just said what I have going to say. If the Prosecution makes their objection -- well, we've heard the objection. But if they keep repeating this objection, then I must take this to be tactics to take up more time and fanning the flames here in this discussion. I think that an objection in principle was in order. The Trial Chamber is not sleeping. The Trial Chamber is vigilant. It is listening, and it set the guidelines for Praljak, and we have the practice established in this courtroom over the past year. And I'm quite sure that the Trial Chamber is qualified to be able to assess the situation without interference from the Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber is very well able to state that this goes outside the guidelines or it is within the guidelines set. So it is my proposal that the Prosecution refrain from taking the floor all the time. You have set the standards, and you are there to control those standards, to see that they are put into practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the technical questions of road blockings, since Mr. Praljak had command responsibility, he was at that time in the position to order checkpoints to be set up or removed. He does have technical competence and may, therefore, speak of these roadblocks. Now, Mr. Praljak, you may proceed. Ask your question but try to stick to simple questions, technical ones. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very simple. Does the lady know that Slobodan Praljak was the initiator and partially the organiser to make this route possible and to save the refugees from being persecuted by the Serbs? I'm just asking the witness whether she knows about that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were in the Mostar in June and saw that Mostar had been liberated, do you know who the commander of the operation to liberate Mostar was?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Jasmin Jaganjac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Turbe and Travnik and its importance for the defence of Travnik, because otherwise the Serbs could reach Sarajevo through the Lasva River Valley. Now my question is this: Did you know the organisation -- that I took over the organisation of the defence of Travnik and set up the HVO and -- and was the first of among equals, if I can say that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when I -- when this critical point was, I mean in autumn 1992, I was already testifying that the cooperation with the Croats, with the HVO and Muslim army was very well. And I was myself living in HVO headquarters, so I knew that they were defending Turbe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, did you ever personally see Ivan Drnis?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought to see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I apologise for having to interrupt, but there are time constraints. So just say, "No, I never saw him," and I'll move on. Now, to ask you about the electric power plants. Tell me this, madam, do you know how many electric power plants there are from Rama, Prozor, to Mostar? How many power plants are there?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know surely, but I think at least five.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Jablanica the largest electric power plant or not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say you talked to Hadzihasanovic, and then you say later on he became Chief of Staff of the BH army. Did you know that Hadzihasanovic never became the chief of the Main Staff of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so it was told me. I met him once more in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw some sort of refugee camp in Posusje. Do you know that, at the end of the summer and beginning of the autumn 1992, the HZ HB received, in Posusje, 25.000 refugees, Muslim refugees, and that they weren't camps. They were just places where people had been taken in, and they were helped in various ways? Are you aware of those figures and that fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak, I must intervene. The President has given a ruling. He has told you on which subjects you may ask questions, because according to the rules, you can exceptionally ask questions on specific points. What you are doing is that you totally disregard what the is President has told you and simply ask any questions that you think you would like to ask, questions that are not technical at all, technical questions of the type that all counsel for the other accused asked themselves. And it is not to be seen why in this case your excellent counsel could not ask all these questions. You are simply disregarding the rules of the game, and I would ask you to comply with them. And if questions that you would like to have asked are not such exceptional questions, then I'm sure Mr. Kovacic will do this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, are you forcing me not to ask these questions? Let's clarify the situation to the end. Judge Trechsel, I worked on this -- these things. I was there. I know what the problems are with the tents and everything else. The lady said that these were camps. So I do have the right, in my quest for the truth, to ask these very precise questions without taking up anybody else's time, because I have every right to justice. I don't have to entreat you for justice. It is my right to be accorded justice, and it will help us arrive at the truth. So if you prohibit me to ask these questions, then I will make some other decisions. I'm asking precise figures. I'm not delving into other matters because she talks about the 1939 or other years, who the Hungarians were, who -- what belonged to whom. So I'm no third-rate scholar. I have the right to defend myself. I cooperate with and collaborate with Mr. Kovacic. But as to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, what the situation was there, what the Territorial Defence, what the banovinas were, who Sreta [phoen] was, who Marcek was, who Stradinovic [phoen] was. This is the field that I have been devoting my work to for the past 40 years. So please allow me to conclude my discussion here with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Praljak. These are not the rules of this game. It is not for you to say definitely what your rights are and what you need, but it's for the Trial Chamber; and if someone does not agree there's a possibility of an appeal, and that has been done here. And I invite you, perhaps with the assistance of your counsel, to carefully study the decision which was recently handed out by the Chamber of Appeal, and you will see that the Chamber of Appeal entirely supports this Trial Chamber's ruling that you are not allowed to do your own cross-examination and ask any questions that you think it is useful to ask. And the issue is not whether you are able to ask such questions, but it's, rather, the other way around. The right for the accused to put questions themselves is reserved for cases where counsel would not be able, exceptionally, to effectively conduct the cross-examination. Now, I cannot see how Mr. Kovacic would not be able to ask the questions you are asking. The Chamber had decided that you could ask questions on electricity - and I think you have done that. Perhaps you have more of them - and on the HOS. And it is simply disobedience if you do not comply with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I share my colleague's opinion. The problem which you do not seem to understand is that the Chamber has come to a decision which has been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. That decision is that the rights of an accused to ask his own questions is limited. Because if the lawyer is in a position to ask the questions, then the accused must only ask the remaining questions, those that go beyond the competence of the lawyer. What you should have done is, before the hearing, you should have shared subjects out with your counsel. The counsel could have asked all general questions, and you could have stuck to the ultra-technical matters. We would not be in this situation if you had. Obviously, in matters of electricity, for example, you're more competent than Mr. Kovacic, and it may also be so when it comes to the HOS. But when it comes to humanitarian convoys or other such matters, your counsel could have been asking those questions as well of you. The difficult thing now is to distinguish between what is really technical and what your counsel could be asking. As far as I'm concerned, and as you know, I have never prohibited you from asking a few questions, but I am a member of a Bench. I am not alone, and there is majority of Judges here that have a very specific position to which I have to stand by. Now, if you insist on defending your service, you have another possibility, which is to say that you don't want to have a counsel for the Defence, and that you want to defend yourself, but this is something that might be disadvantageous to you. Now, there is one technical matter still to be dealt with: The HOS. And the Bench allows you to ask questions about the HOS. Once that is done, Mr. Kovacic will have the floor to ask those questions which you had remaining on your list. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance, Your Honour. Since this is the very first day that we're enforcing this decision, and given that I -- I just want to try to find a solution because we have limited time. Perhaps, today, we could make some allowances; but from henceforth now, there is a clear warning from the Bench as far as how Mr. Praljak and Mr. Kovacic are to work this out among themselves. So I think it might be good since -- otherwise, I don't believe Mr. Kovacic would be able to do the sort of job that Mr. Praljak has prepared himself, and only himself, to do. So I think that, in all fairness, since it is a new ruling, perhaps we can make an exception today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one small point, and I am grateful to my colleague for his proposal, but there is another aspect that needs to be mentioned here, because actually my colleagues from the Prosecution and Judge Trechsel have mentioned this several times. The recent Appeals Chamber decision, dated the 10th of May, changed nothing in relation to your previous decision dating from April. It fully upheld your decision. And in your decision in which you modified to a certain extent the Guideline C --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I was referring to an Appeals Chamber decision of, I think, 24th of August. August, not May, not 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I do apologise, Your Honour. It is my mistake, but also partially a mistake in translation. That's the decision that we received last week. So I maintain that this decision of the Appeals Chamber does not change the previous decision of this Trial Chamber. It upholds your previous decision, and your latest decision that we appealed was just a revision of your previous decision, the Guideline C decision from last year. So I see no reason why we should actually change our practice. You did allow General Praljak to cross-examine on certain matters. We have the parameters in place in this courtroom. We have the practice in this courtroom. And since your last decision was slightly more restrictive than the previous one, but the practice remained in practice, the examination could proceed on rather broad principles. I see no reason why we should actually change the practice, because the Appeals Chamber decision upheld your decision. And I believe that what General Praljak wanted to ask is well within the sphere of what is allowed, bearing in mind the decisions of other Trial Chambers that are referred to by the Appeals Chamber, and bearing in mine the practice before this Tribunal and the general principle that the accused is not an object but a subject of proceedings. You of course always prevent him from asking questions, prohibit him from asking questions, but this would mark a 180-degree turn in relation to the practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In first hearing the questions from the accused that came after the Trial Chamber issued its ruling, and now listening to the comments of Mr. Praljak's counsel, it's abundantly clear, in our view, that Mr. Praljak and his Defence intend to just continue on in exactly the same way that they have in all prior cross-examinations. That ignores the fact that we now have a decision of this Trial Chamber, which has been affirmed by the Appeals Chamber. The Prosecution has been less than forceful in pressing or asking the Trial Chamber to enforce its earlier decision. Now that we have the Appeal decision, however, Mr. President, we are going to continue to object when, in our view, the decision of this Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber is not being respected, because, ultimately, this is a matter of an accused respecting decision of the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. What's being proposed here is that those decisions being disregarded, and we're going to continue to object. We cannot enforce the Court's rulings, only the Trial Chamber can do that, but we're going to continue to object, and more frequently than we have in the past, now that the Appeals Chamber has clearly approved the Trial Chamber's procedures on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the suggestion from Mr. Karnavas is that the Chamber could choose to be flexible, given that the decision of the Chamber's appeal is recent and that the Defence has not had time to adapt to it and that we ought to be flexible. Under these conditions, the Bench, having duly considered, and exceptionally for this day only, are going to allow Mr. Praljak to ask his questions. In the future, Mr. Praljak and his counsel are going to have to share out the jobs in conformity with the decision respectively of this Chamber and the Chamber of Appeal, because, otherwise, we're going to waste a tremendous amount of time. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor again. Please be quick. The Chamber, recognising that this is the first time that the decision of the Appeals Chamber is being enforced, and you have not been in a position to conduct with your counsel, we are giving you the floor again, and you may ask your questions. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will go through my questions very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, was the HOS a party formation of the HSP, the Croatian Party of Rights?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to what you knew, were there more Muslims in the HOS ranks than Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. According to your knowledge, was the HOS recognised by President Alija Izetbegovic as the regular formation of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was paramilitary troop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that all the -- all HOS units became part of the BH army afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that Mostar was under siege. Did you know the lines of the HVO, the Republika Srpska army, and the BH army at that time when you claim Mostar was under siege?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not there because it was not possible, but anyway --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't have enough time, so please no explanations, just tell me: "I was there." "I was not there." But could you please tell me the following: Do you know, madam, the Mostar municipality, after the Croat-Muslim conflict, was -- did the BH army control more of the Mostar municipality than the HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were controlling it together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's true. But did the BH army control more of the Mostar municipality than the HVO or not? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western part was controlled from HVO; eastern part from the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, greater or lesser part of the municipality, who held which, in territorial terms?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the boundaries of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. You said that while you were in Vitez that you saw some kind of a howitzer or a cannon firing at Zenica. Do you know anything about artillery?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know what it was. It was howitzer from 155 millimetre, and its name was "Nora," and it was brought before to the UNPROFOR headquarters. Everybody could see it. But at that time, when I was there, it was in a stone mine about three kilometres behind us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you at the quarry or stone mine?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have all reasons to believe that from the BritBat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you whether you were at the quarry or stone mine, so please don't talk to me about the trust that you had in the British Battalion. But when you said -- when you saw the charge or the elevation of the barrel, were you able to determine what this Nora 155-millimetre was actually targeting? Were you able to determine the target that this howitzer was firing on, on the basis of the elevation, charge, and other elements? Are you able to conclude that or not?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an artillery officer, but it was still the shelling to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you see the shelling of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Further, you said that the anti-aircraft artillery fired on a Muslim village where there were civilians. What's the name of that village where there were civilians? Did you visit the village? Did you know what the village was called?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the village, but I don't remember all these names any more, but it was in the area of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said also that a mercenary had told you he had been arrested because he had a beard and Croats thought he was a Chetnik, and that that was the reason why he had been arrested. Do you know that at the time, when he was arrested, I was the chief of the HVO Main Staff? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that I had a beard at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but not that kind of beard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that I was actually arrested because I had a beard, and it was possible that I was a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many troops the BH army had in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many troops the BH army had in the spring of 1993; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which region you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the strength of the -- the manpower of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many troops the HVO had in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the -- that Sefer Halilovic, the chief of the Main Staff of the BH army stated in Geneva that it had 250.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am convinced that I always asked quite specific technical questions that clarified the situation and that discussed the issues that I know of, and my questions regarding the refugees stem from the fact that I tried my best to help those people, and I know more about that than any counsel. I can of course allow my counsel to ask some more questions, but I don't see what would happen, how that might improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one question that stems from a question asked by my colleague. I don't want to take up my learned colleague's time. It has to do with the date of the interview with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you said you were in Vitez and that BritBat briefed you on the situation in Ahmici. You said that there were two representatives of the UN Security Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Four. You can't give us the exact date, but you said that it had to be sometime between the 22nd and the 24th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And depending on when this event took place, we could deduce the date if we were able to discover when these people were there, because you said, "I cannot pinpoint the time, but that was on the day when the representatives of the UN Security Council were there in Ahmici"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me then ask you this, and we can use other documents to pinpoint this: Do you remember any of the names of the UN Security Council representatives that might help us later on to determine this?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, how much time are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, one minute. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to use my half hour, but if my colleague needs some time to conclude this issue I will let him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that the witness would be consulting her documents. I am happy that she did so, but I have to ask her what those documents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, madam, which documents did you just refer to?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is my article about Ahmici, and here is the picture of some agency, and here is the picture of Venezuelan representative, and here is told that his name was Diego Arria. It is from 26th of fourth, 1993. So it's something I have been writing but the picture is not from me because it was not possible to send pictures from Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one question in this regard, then. The gentleman you just mentioned, do you know that he was an investigator with Mazowiecki's commission, not a representative of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it was told that he was the UN ambassador of Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But do you know who presented him in this way? Did he introduce himself in this manner or did somebody else do that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already that he was represented to us as a representative of UN Security Council from Bob Stewart, the BritBat commandant, but now this title which I have here, it is from some international news agency because the picture is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. So you're just saying that you link this date with this event. You are sure about the date because of this event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure that it was all in the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot explore this matter any further. Only we did not receive this article from the Prosecution. The Prosecution may have gotten it, but we would appreciate if we could get a copy at the end of the testimony perhaps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. We have precious little time, and I will start asking you questions right away. If I understand you correctly, you did not have any knowledge about the events in Ahmici prior to your interview with Mr. Prlic and during this interview. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your first question to Mr. Prlic, as we can see from the text of the interview, pertains to armed conflicts between the HVO and the BH army. Could you please tell us which conflicts did you have in mind when you asked this question?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was already yesterday explaining that we knew that there is a conflict. We knew it from a Bosnian journalist and from Ed Vulliamy, but I didn't know any exact happenings -- happenings, and the name Ahmici was not familiar to me. I knew that there were tensions between these two armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what fighting were you asking him about? What fighting did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was since January some fightings within -- I meant fightings between HVO and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting you. Let's forget about January now. We're in April 1993 now. So you did not refer to the events in January. You were asking questions about the current situation. So in your first question you ask about the fighting going on at that time, and you are asking about the actual current situation, the situation as of the day when the interview was taking place. So what fighting were you asking Mr. Prlic about?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, the fighting in Mostar. I was told the day before that there was fighting, and I was collecting casualties everywhere there. I could see that there had been very much shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Except the fighting in Mostar, you were talking about fighting in plural. So what other fighting did you mean when you were asking this question of Mr. Prlic? Can we agree that you actually didn't know that at the time when you were talking to Mr. Prlic there was any fighting between the HVO and the BH army? Would I be correct if I were to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take these questions from the air, but the situation I knew -- exact situation I knew first afterwards, I had second-hand knowledge from Ed Vulliamy and the Bosnian journalist that there had been fightings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, this is precisely what I'm talking about, what you knew at the time of the interview and what you learned afterwards. I would like to clear up those details. Can we agree that at the time when you were interviewing Mr. Prlic you didn't know any details about military conflicts, armed conflicts, between the BH army and the HVO? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's so, because I was just on the way to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. At the time when you were doing the interview, you had knowledge of the alleged ultimatum that was issued to Alija Izetbegovic. Could you please tell us, where were you at the beginning of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you learned about this alleged ultimatum from the Austrian press which published a Reuters report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You had no other knowledge about the contents of the alleged ultimatum, is that correct, apart from this source?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was discussing about this ultimatum with the leader of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian army, Hadzihasanovic, but he didn't take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did he give you any other significant information additional to what was reported by the Reuters about the contents of the alleged ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, madam, in one of your texts which the Prosecutor showed us, 2094, Exhibit 2094, in your analysis there, you said, on page 5 of the English text, that everything began with Boban's ultimatum of the 15th of April, and that the Muslims did not hand over their arms. Can we agree that that is what you said, that that is the contents of your report?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, if we take a look at the Reuters report, document P 1804, no mention is made there any where that the contents of that alleged ultimatum was the surrender of arms by the BH army to the HVO. But since we don't have enough time for you to read the Reuters report, try and do your best to remember. Where did you get this information from that anybody in April 1993 asked somebody else to surrender their arms to them? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "surrender" was mentioned in nowhere. It was only mentioned that two possibilities: To hand up the arms or to be under HVO command. It means that, in certain areas, the Muslim troops should be under HVO command. And I have already told many times that these two options were there. Which was true? I don't know. Because that is now the question of interpretation, how the ultimatum was interpreted: That the Muslims were under HVO or that they give their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not interpreting anything. We're trying to establish the facts: What the contents of the Reuters report was and what you wrote. Now, we'll all be able to establish for ourselves what was actually said, but would you try and think about this. Are you perhaps mixing up the contents of something that was also referred to as an ultimatum in January 1993 with what was also called an ultimatum in April 1993? Could you perhaps have mixed the two up? Just give me a simple answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You're not mixing these things up: The difference between the contents of one alleged ultimatum and the contents of the other alleged ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's impossible because I didn't know any ultimatum in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your article, and you spoke about this yesterday, you said that, on the 16th of April, after the ultimatum had expired, the deadline had expired, that everything began after that, that there were a series of HVO attacks against the BH army units, and that all this was synchronised in such a way that the only logical conclusion was that there was an order for attack from the top. And this was recorded in yesterday's transcript on page 89. Did I understand you correctly? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now tell us this, please, Witness: If you, at a time when you're conducting an interview with Mr. Prlic, don't know about any fighting between the BH army and the HVO, how then can you conclude that, on the 16th of April, a series of synchronised attacks began or tell us, or rather, tell was what were these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. I was writing these articles after interview with Mr. Prlic. And the one who was telling that this was synchronised attacks everywhere, his name is Bob Stewart, the colonel the BritBat, and he was telling that all publicly in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us a moment ago, with respect to Mr. Prlic's letter complaining about the bias in the media, you said that the British media were indeed biased to a certain extent, and that from the very outset that they were a little antagonistic towards Herceg-Bosna. Isn't that right? That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It's also interesting to note that of the journalists that testified of in this courtroom, they were all British journalists, with the exception of yourself and another man from the former Yugoslavia. Now, tell me, is it just by chance that it -- that it was the British media who were biased, or was there a system involved in this, some sort of system, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a certain system, and I can tell you what this system was. It was all the same which all UNPROFOR troop where was, but the pressman was always British, especially, because in Vitez there was a British Battalion, there were plenty of British journalists. So when I was visiting Ahmici, it was maybe 20 British journalists, and I, and Erich, and one Spanish one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you received information from the British press service in the battalion, right, in BritBat?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from BritBat. I didn't believe everything. But -- but military matters, yes, they know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think we've dealt with that. Now, you asked Mr. Prlic a question about the fighting between the BH army and the HVO, and he answered and mentioned the fighting in Konjic. From the other question about Konjic, I make the conclusion that you did not know that at that time there was some fighting going on in Konjic. Would I be right in making that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, and that's why I was asking him Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to show you a document so that you can see when the fighting in Konjic actually started, and this may perhaps refresh your memory and show you some new aspects. So look at document 4D 438. It's in my binder. It's a very short report by the commander of a brigade of the BH army. The brigade's name was the Suad Alic Brigade from Konjic, and the Trial Chamber has already seen this report on a number of occasions. But anyway, a commander of the Muslim army is informing the 4th Corps, that is to say, his superiors, about the situation in Konjic and says the following: "150 members of the HVO captured, the town blocked, life in the town paralysed. We continue with the arrests." And the report was received in the 4th Corps on the 24th of March, 1993? Tell us, please, Witness, did you have any knowledge, to the effect that at the end of March, offensive actions by the BH army started against the HVO in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Konjic area, and I was no knowledge about this kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness, and -- or rather, do you feel you know something only if you were personally in the area where this was happening, or do you think that you know about something if you learnt it from someone else or from the media?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best is always to see yourself. Of course, I can believe also something what I learned from somebody else, but then I need several sources, not only one. Never trust one source.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, from any source, following the Croatian press, as you said, did you gain any knowledge about offensive actions by the BH army on the territory of Konjic already at the end of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in March 1993 in Croatia. I was in Vienna. So I was not following -- I was not all the time in the area. I was just coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you have any knowledge to the effect that, with respect to the fighting in and around Konjic, that certain HVO forces were involved from the territory of the operative zone, if you know what that means, of South-east Herzegovina and North-west Herzegovina -- or, rather, units from the surrounding areas? Do you have any knowledge or awareness about that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have knowledge from Konjic. That's why I was also asking Mr. Prlic that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you have any knowledge to the effect that some time before mid-April 1993, the BH army in Zenica captured a large number of soldiers belonging to the HVO? About 600 HVO soldiers, in fact. Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have very little time left, so I'm going to have to move on to another area, and that is the subject of Prozor. You told us that, in November 1992, you passed through Prozor; and in the statement that you gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, you said that you arrived in Prozor after, and I'll quote, "the attack by the HVO against local Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. November 1992, there was no hostilities between HVO and Bosnian army. They were together defending -- defending Turbe, but there was some problem. But it was in Jajce area, and it has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So may we then conclude that, in the Prozor area, there was no -- or rather, there was not any kind of armed conflict between the HVO and the BH army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, I didn't see any. It was quite normal in -- in November, and I was passing Prozor twice and going to Central Bosnia and coming back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In January 1993, were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina then?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but my mission was little bit longer. As I told yesterday, I started in Banja Luka and Jajce. I was visiting when the Serbs captured Jajce and Banja Luka, and -- and then I have to go back to Zagreb and go around the coast to get then to Central Bosnia. I was very near Central Bosnia; but from Jajce, there was no possibility to go through, you know. There was the Serbian front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us, madam, if I understood you correctly, that in January 1993, the fighting started between the HVO and the BH army after the proclamation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you also said that the fighting began in Gornji Vakuf and Busovaca; right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any other area in which there were armed -- there was armed fighting between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were the two ones which I -- which I saw still at that time when I went in February to Central Bosnia, and there was armistice. It was told it was armistice. It was calmed down, but it didn't look like that in Gornji Vakuf. In Busovaca, it was peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the conflict in Busovaca. Do you know who launched the offensive in Busovaca and why?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, it's the same story as other where, because taking over these areas which were promised us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that the following month, that is to say, in February 1993, you talked to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, in your statement, you said that he tried to explain to you that the attack against Busovaca was provoked by the BH army, but that you did not believe him because that, quite simply, was not logical. And that is to be found in your statement in the English text page 3, last paragraph. Now, in this connection, I'd like to ask you the following: Do you know exactly -- do you know what the meaning of Busovaca was in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was also on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I mean, in the communicational sense, as a communications line.

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was no traffic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at another document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I truly apologise to Ms. Alaburic. I would just like to inform the Court that the Prosecution would have only about three or four minutes that we would require that for examination -- re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the question I was about to put to you. Ms. Alaburic, you have two come to a close now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to withdraw that question because the maps will be able to rule on the importance of Busovaca by comparing the maps. But what I want to ask you is this: The representatives of the Herzegovinians in the parliament of the Republic of Croatia. Now, you referred to this yesterday, and you said from that one can see the pretensions that the Republic of Croatia had vis-a-vis the area of Herzegovina. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from that. There was also very many Herzegovinians in government: Vladimir Seks, Gojko Susak, the defence minister, and so on. There was a very clear connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, Vladimir Seks is from the heart of Slavonia, from Osijek, but that's not important at this point. I assume that you did not read the electoral laws of the Republic of Croatia. You haven't read those, have you?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I read it always for election, and it was election for 1995. And the Herzegovinians were for the first time to be allowed to vote and be in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Do you know that the Croatian constitution, just like the constitutions of any other country, stipulates that all adults have the right to vote, all inhabitants of age, which means that they have the right to elect and to be elected? Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, if a Croatian citizen finds themselves in Holland, France, or Bosnia-Hercegovina, for instance, then that citizen also has the right to vote or to elect and be elected? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a citizen is in Holland, he has moved to Holland and, as I understand, still has Croatian documents. But the citizens of Western Herzegovina have been there hundreds of years. It was just that I know that they had so-called double citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, all I want to ask you is this: Is it a rule that the citizen of one country enjoys all the rights that he would have in that country, and that nobody has the right to curtail his civic rights, regardless of where that person might be at any given point in time? That's a physical matter, where he's going to vote. But if he is a national of a country, the citizen of a country, then he enjoys full electoral rights in that country. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not correct for a neighbouring country where they're given these citizen rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If there is the possibility of somebody having dual citizenship, then from the aspects of citizenship in one country, in this case the Republic of Croatia, then he is the citizen of that country with absolutely full rights. So dual citizenship affords this citizen the same rights as a citizen who has just won citizenship. Isn't that right? Can we agree there on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: ... constitution law. That's surely legal questions of comparative law and they're not obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is very logical question. And for a witness such as this one who is educated in history, in politics and who was a journalist and who has testified here about the Herzegovinians in the Croatian parliament and endeavoured to link up Zagreb and Herzegovina in that respect, then the question is a very logical one. I won't insist further because I respect the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But I'd just like to say that yesterday you told us, madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be just allowed one more question, please, just one more question. One final question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about the Croatian media yesterday and what media were independent. You told us that the Nedeljna Dalmacija newspaper was an independent paper that you could rely on, if I understood you correctly. Now, my question is: Are you -- are you certain is that it was Nedeljna Dalmacija that you were referring to and not the Herald Tribune perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Feral Tribune.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is a political weekly?

utterances.speaker: MARITA VIHERVUORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen that kind of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Only one issue to raise with the assistance of the usher -- with the registry if we could call up on the e-court Exhibit P 01155. P 01155. This was a document admitted on 12 June 2007, if we may just have the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Madam, this was a decision that was signed by Mr. Jadranko Prlic on 15 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. It's beyond the scope of the direct examination, as well as the cross-examination. Now, if the gentleman wish -- she indicated, first of all, that she knew nothing about any ultimatum in January. That is first and foremost. Secondly, now he's trying to go into another area. If he's allowed, then I should be allowed to do recross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One question as part of redirect should be in line with questions put during the cross-examination. So please remind us of the question put by the Defence, and then you can show us your document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is in a direct response to a question posed by Ms. Alaburic during her cross-examination, regarding an ultimatum in January 1993 and whether there was any confusion about this. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, this decision, I only want to direct your attention to item 1 which states: "All units of the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
